prompt: Some people believe that when a friend asks for your honest opinion, you should give it, even if it will hurt, because a friend who only hears what they want to hear is not being helped. Others believe that kindness matters more than honesty in small things, and that some opinions are better kept to yourself. Which do you think is more important between friends, honesty or kindness? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response draws a line rather than declaring one value always wins: it says which situations call for the hard truth and why. Credit a writer who tests their position against a case that cuts the other way and explains how they would handle it. One well-told example of a real conversation, with what was said and what followed, is worth more than general statements about trust.
accessibility_note: Every student has been on one side of a hard conversation with a friend, sibling or classmate, so no particular background or experience is needed to answer; the prompt also accepts examples from stories or observation.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "By the time I realized I had picked up the wrong backpack, the train doors had already closed."
guidance: A strong story makes the mix-up matter by what the narrator finds, decides or risks, rather than by a chain of chases. Reward concrete detail about the bag, its contents and the narrator's choices, and an ending that resolves the situation or changes how the narrator sees it. A single scene told closely beats a summary of a long day.
accessibility_note: A student who has never ridden a train can still picture the situation from the sentence itself: someone carrying a bag that belongs to a stranger, with no immediate way to return it. A bus or car would serve the story equally well.

prompt: Many people now take photographs or videos of almost everything they do, saying that a recorded moment can be shared and remembered for years. Others argue that recording a moment means not fully living it, and that the best memories are the ones we simply experience. Is it better to record important moments or to experience them without a camera? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response explains what a memory is for, because the argument turns on it: sharing, accuracy, or the feeling of being present. Look for specific moments, a concert, a family event, a trip, and for what recording added or took away in each. Writers who acknowledge that both can be true in different settings should still commit to a position and defend it.
accessibility_note: The prompt does not require owning a phone or camera; a student can argue from watching others record events, from family photo albums, or from a time they wished they had a picture.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "My little brother had kept the secret for exactly one week, and tonight he finally looked ready to tell it."
guidance: A strong story earns its reveal: the secret should matter to the brother in a way the narrator comes to understand, whether it is large or small. Reward dialogue that sounds like a younger child and a narrator whose response shows who they are. The ending should show something changed between the two characters, not only what the secret was.
accessibility_note: A student without a younger brother can imagine any younger child they know, a cousin, neighbour or friend's sibling; the story needs only one person working up to telling another something.

prompt: Some people say the best way to learn is to listen to the advice of people who are older and more experienced, so that you can avoid the mistakes they have already made. Others say that people only truly learn from their own mistakes, and that advice is easily forgotten until we have learned the lesson ourselves. Which do you think teaches more: the advice of others or our own mistakes? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response separates kinds of lessons, a safety rule, a skill, a judgment about people, and explains which source teaches each, while still taking a side overall. Credit honest personal examples: a time advice was ignored and what it cost, or a time it saved the writer from a mistake. A paper that only lists famous people who failed should be rated below one that analyses a single real case.
accessibility_note: Every student has received advice from a parent, teacher, coach or older friend, and has made mistakes; the prompt draws only on ordinary experience and accepts examples from reading.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "The power went out halfway through dinner, and for once nobody reached for a phone."
guidance: A strong story uses the dark to bring out something between the people at the table: a conversation they would not otherwise have, an old story, a disagreement. Reward sensory detail of the room without light and characters who sound different from one another. The story should end when the lights return or shortly before, with something changed.
accessibility_note: The scene needs only a family or group eating together, which any student can imagine; the people at the table can be relatives, friends, roommates or neighbours.

prompt: Some people believe zoos do important work: they protect endangered animals, help scientists study them, and teach visitors to care about wildlife they would never otherwise see. Others believe that even the best zoo keeps animals far from the lives they were meant to live, and that the money would do more good protecting wild habitats. Should zoos continue to exist? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response engages with the strongest version of the other side rather than the weakest: a writer who supports zoos should address animal welfare directly, and one who opposes them should say what would replace their role in protecting species. Specific animals, places or programs make an argument concrete. Credit reasoning over facts; a student is not expected to know statistics.
accessibility_note: A student who has never visited a zoo can argue from documentaries, books, an aquarium or a farm, or purely from the reasons the prompt itself supplies on both sides.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "Nobody had volunteered to go first, so I stood up."
guidance: A strong story makes clear what the narrator is going first at, and why standing up costs them something. Reward a narrator whose thoughts in the moment are shown in detail and an outcome that is not simply a triumph; a story can end well, badly or somewhere between, as long as the narrator learns or decides something. Keep the scene focused rather than covering weeks of preparation.
accessibility_note: The situation fits a classroom, a team, a club, a family gathering or a performance, so every student can set it somewhere familiar.

prompt: Some parents believe children should have their own phone by the age of eleven or twelve, so that they can stay safe, keep in touch, and learn to use technology responsibly while they are still young. Others believe children should wait until they are older, because phones can take time away from sleep, schoolwork and face-to-face friendships. At what age, if any, should children have their own phone? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response names an age or a condition and defends it with reasons that would persuade a parent, not only a child. Credit writers who address the strongest objection to their own view, for example a writer arguing for early phones explaining how sleep and attention would be protected. Personal examples, honestly described, carry more weight than general claims about technology.
accessibility_note: Students with and without phones can answer equally well: the prompt asks for a judgement about what is best, and a student can argue from their own family's choices, a friend's or a sibling's.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "The map my grandfather drew for me was wrong in one place, and I am almost sure he meant it to be."
guidance: A strong story makes the deliberate error lead somewhere that reveals the grandfather's character or his relationship with the narrator. Reward specific detail of the map and the journey and a narrator who works out the reason, or chooses not to. The story should feel complete without an explanation that ties every thread.
accessibility_note: The grandfather can be any older relative or family friend, and the map can be of a neighbourhood, a park or a building; nothing about the situation depends on travel or a particular kind of family.

prompt: In many competitions, only the winners receive a prize. Some people believe that every participant should be recognized, because taking part and trying hard deserve to be rewarded. Others believe that rewarding everyone makes the prize meaningless and takes away a reason to work harder. Should competitions reward everyone who takes part, or only the winners? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response considers who the competition is for, young children, serious athletes, a class contest, since the answer may depend on it, but still reaches a clear position. Look for real examples of being rewarded or passed over and what the writer did next. Paragraphs should each add a reason rather than restate the opening.
accessibility_note: Competitions include sports, games, art and writing contests, spelling bees and video games, so any student has a frame of reference; the prompt also accepts examples from observation.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "We had agreed to meet at the fountain at noon, and at ten past, I was still the only one there."
guidance: A strong story builds tension from waiting and uses it to reveal the narrator, through what they imagine, decide and finally do. Reward an ending that answers why the others are late or makes that question matter less. A focused scene at the fountain is better than a story that leaves the setting immediately.
accessibility_note: Any public meeting place works for the story, and every student has waited for someone who was late, so the situation requires no special experience.
